The AARTO Amendment Act - Are You Ready?

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Amendment to the AARTO Act, currently only covering Johannesburg and Tshwane, will become countrywide on July 1st and stakeholders are warning of total gridlock and damaging life consequences.

Unique Selling Point:
Because it's a pilot phase the points demerit system of the AARTO system doesn't apply yet, the Minister of Transport has not proclaimed the points demerit system to be in force. But this year the Government is instigating a revolution in AARTO, heralded as a mechanism for improving road safety and a way to ease the burden on courts. The Administrative Adjudication of Road Traffic Offences is to be centralized and will adjudicate countrywide. But what it really could mean is, whatever you thought you knew about traffic offences, think again.
The Amendment to the AARTO Act, which currently only has jurisdiction in Johannesburg and Tshwane, is timetabled to be rolled out on July 1st 2021 and automobile stakeholders are warning of total bureaucratic gridlock and damaging life consequences brought on by a skewed system driven by revenue collection, as opposed to road safety.

Summary:
Currently in Johannesburg and Tswane they have been recording demerit points but not enforcing any consequences regarding the points although fines for traffic infringements still have to be paid. So for our story - the consequences regarding the demerit points system have to be hypothetical at this stage, but we do have real life case studies that will show how their current infringements, be they actual or erroneous as in the incorrect number plate case study, could mean under the demerits point sytem and it's administrative pitfalls they would have their licences suspended.

Re-enactment
August 2021. Mr Joe Soap travels this road every day to and from work. He doesn't realize, because of inadequate notices, that last week the JMPD changed the speed limit of a short stretch of her route from 80 to 60 kilometres per hour. In 40 working days he will have racked up R 56 000 in fines (not to mention the R 100 payment, the Infringement Penalty Levy (IPL),for the privilege of receiving each fine) and 80 demerit points, enough to be banned from driving for 16 and a quarter years. All because there is a speed camera there and it can take up to 60 days for the notification of offences (if they arrive). The AARTO amendments is a strict consequence-based points system.

The AARTO Act has effectively three documents
1. Infringement notice, recording the offence
2. Courtesy letter, a reminder to pay
3. Enforcement order, recording the offences consequences and non-payment penalties
There are no Warrants of Arrest, no Administration Marks.


Further information:
Skewed penalties and Life Consequences
As Howard Dembovsky (of Justice Project South Africa) says, before you even become aware of the fact that that you've been committing traffic offences your license is gone. On the other hand, the drunk driver who drives slowly, because he's trying to follow the dotted lines on the road, he doesn't build up these speeding demerit points, rather he needs to get arrested and convicted nine times before he loses his license.
And what of Joe Soap's right to appeal? Well, The AARTO Amendment's appeal process is governed by a tribunal panel of 9 people, at least six of which sit for each appeal. These nine cover the whole country, 13 million driving license holders and a further 13 million registered vehicles. A recipe for Gridlock if people realize that if they appeal every notice of infringement there is no way the Tribunal Panel can keep up. So the claim that AARTO will take the strain off of the courts, really means it just transfers the pressure to another body, it's own Tribunal system. Nine people to do the work of 749 lower courts!
And there's more, like, you buy a vehicle from a person and pay them good money for it. And then you can't register the vehicle in your name. Why? Because it can't be taken out of the seller's name because licensing transactions are blocked by an AARTO enforcement order.
Also, it is the Insurance Companies' plan to access your demerit points as the insured person and adjust your premium according to the number of demerit points that you have. But when when your insurance premiums become unaffordable, are you going to continue being insured, so the 35% of drivers currently insured may well drop in number.

Extra information
We will highlight other scenarios that highlight the discrepancy between preaching road safety but practicing maximizing revenue. Like, the R 3000 fine for not updating authorities on where you live, compared with a R 500 fine and 1 demerit point for transporting your baby by car without sitting them safely in a car baby chair. Howard Dembovsky has a database of all the offences and consequences for us to access further comparisons of the weighting of certain offenses.
Are there alternative solutions? Howard Dembovsky suggests: scrap the AARTO Act and incorporate the points demerit system into the National Road Traffic Act and establish a dedicated 24 hours per day traffic court.
Howard Dembovsky is also willing to surprise the presenter by revealing to them their current traffic offenses record and the consequences of those under the AARTO Act Amendment.
Possible case study:

Older Lady - Gladys Rankhumise - Mini bus taxis were registered in her name without her knowledge: Enforcement orders issued against her in respect of those mini bus taxis prevented her from renewing her driver's licence. Under the demerit system she would also not have been aware that these demerits were notching up against her name, because they were being sent to a false address. In this instance she filled in the prescribed form, submited it to the agency for consideration, they rejected her submission, and had she not been able to get someone to help her argue her case, like Howard, she would have to get herself a lawyer, because under the new system once an enforecement order has been issued you can no longer apply to the tribunal for appeal. She would have to institute a PAJA application to the high court, which would cost her no less than a million Rand. Under the new system.. once the enforcement order has been issued she is left with two options either pay the outstanding enforcement orders, which she was not actually liable for which maybe amounted to, say R5000 or R 7000 or pay for the High Court and find a million Rand. Most people would opt for option 1, even if they were not at fault.

Possible Case study:

Kim: (wants her identity hidden, but her boyfriend is prepared to speak on camera)

Stopped at a JMPD road block forced to pay R750,00 which was for an outstanding infringement notice and they wouldn't give back her driver's licence until she paid them immediately. So she went to the police and paid the fine, she got 50% off as the initial fine was for R1500,00 The demerit points applicable to that fine = 5 demerit points. Currently those demerit points are not in force, but the department is apparently monitoring them. Demerit points are applied when you pay the fine, or when you are found guilty in a court of law or when an enforcement order is issued. Demerit points decrease at the rate of 1 point every three months . When she got home after paying the fine, her boyfirend checked her status online and discovered that the fine she paid, was not even for her car and it wasn't even her number plate. The person capturing the data must have misread the number plate, she drives a BMW and the car that was captured was a KIA - her number plate HH and the Kia was HN. But Because she paid the fine and admitted guilt, the demerits are still applied, even if that wasn't her car. The new demerits system which comes into play on the 1st of July would mean that Kim has now notched up 5 demerits and all she needs is another 11 and her license will be suspended for 3 months.

Under the AARTO Act from July 1st, every demerit point over the 15 points threshold means three months license supension. So hypothetically if she received one fine a week for four weeks, with 5 demerit points per fine, by the 4th week her license would be suspended.

Demo 1

With regards to the 80km per hour road that changed to 60 kms for example, we would do this as a demonstration with graphics. There is no case study for this, but it is a good illustration of what would happen to someone driving down a road like that for 40 working days and only received those infringements 60 days later, which is written in the Act that it could take up to 60 days to receive notice of an infringement and this could have the driver's license suspended for 16 and a quarter years.

Demo 2

The additional demonstration we would like to do, either with the presenter or someone who hasn't checked their status, we are looking for possibly a middle aged person who might have their own car and their child's car registered in their name, if they haven't checked their status, they might be in for a huge shock, and when the demerits point system is in force, then for example if most of the infringements were incurred by their child, it doesn't mean the parent or registered owner is off the hook, they are liable and demerits will be applied to their license as well.

I think these are strong illustrations of how if you are unaware of the new laws, you could really be caught short and it could have devastating consequences. If you depend on using your vehicle to get to and from work and your license is suspended for 6 months even, how are you going to earn a living if you can't get there?

Press Release:


The AARTO Amendment Act for administering road traffic offences in South Africa is due for national rollout in July. The new system includes a points demerit system but is it designed to rid our roads of bad drivers or to fill government coffers?

Script:


LINK: South African drivers are familiar with receiving traffic fines,// but some of these fines are never enforced, remain unpaid, or are disputed in a court of law.//

VO: And motorists like this think they can get away with breaking the law.

LINK: On the 1st of July 2021, the AARTO Amendment Act will come into force nationally, changing everything we know about traffic violation enforcement.FX break
Are you ready for the impact?

Fikile Mbalula: - We are going now to implement a demerit system, if you are going to commit a number of offences… you risk losing your drivers licence.

VO: Minister of Transport, Fikile Mbalula, warns South African motorists that they will have to face the strong arm of the law.

Fikile Mbalula: Because in SA motorists have a blank cheque they can do as they wish, it doesn't cost them their licence it doesn't cost them anything.

VO: Howard Dembovsky, Chairperson for the Justice Project South Africa, is a tireless campaigner for ethical and equitable road traffic law and enforcement. He is opposed to the way AARTO, the Administrative Adjudication of Road Traffic Offences, is being implemented.

Howard: What do people ordinarily do when they get a traffic fine in the post? They scrunch it up and throw it in file 13.
Claire: Correct
Howard: But This administrative system, if you do not act, your failure to act then prejudices you.

VO: The JPSA is inundated with requests from motorists unable to sort out their traffic violations like Yulan Chetty,a Joburg resident. He was flummoxed when he couldn't renew his vehicle licence at the post office.

Yulan: I was told to go to the traffic department where I was presented with an A4 sheet of about 24 enforcement orders in my name.
Claire: 24?
Yulan: They were all for the same offence. It was parking outside Gautrain station. it amounted to about R12,000.

VO: Yulan is one of around 4 million drivers who have been guinea pigs under the AARTO pilot study in Joburg and Tshwane since 2008, where traffic violations are categorised into infringements, vetted through an administrative process, and offences - tried through the judicial system.

Howard: So if you caught driving under the influence of alcohol, you're going to be prosecuted in a criminal court.

VO: A parking fine is considered an infringement.

Howard: The most significant part of the AARTO Act is migrating Road Traffic offences out of the realm of criminal courts and into an administrative process, which is unfortunately turned into a huge money making exercise.

Claire: Was there no piece of paper that they left that they said you've got a ticket?
Yulan: There was nothing, nothing.

Claire: What if I do not get that fine in the mail?
Howard: The AARTO act says it's presumed to be served on the tenth day after it's posted. You may make a written representation that the infringement notice was not served on you.

VO: In Yulan’s case, he'd never received infringement notices from the responsible issuing authorities, nor the mandatory courtesy letters from the RTIA, the Road Traffic Infringement Agency. Howard advised Yulan that the only way to appeal was via the AARTO website. And after having to submit 24 certified written representations, eventually all of his fines were revoked.

Yulan: It took me eight months to get my licence. I still had to pay the penalties. Even though the enforcement orders were withdrawn.

Layton: The purpose of AARTO essentially is to improve road safety and to improve compliance amongst drivers. So the principle behind the introduction of AARTO is something that we support.

VO: Layton Beard is the spokesperson for the AA South Africa.

Layton: And the introduction of a demerit system is something that the AA supports, but in its current format, that's where we got the problems that come in.

VO: The legislation provides that If you accrue over 15 demerits your licence gets suspended for three months for each point over 15. Demerits are reduced at 1 point every 3 months. Third strike and you're out. Your licence is cancelled. //
VO: The AA favours a stricter threshold of 12 demerits. They say the proposed amendments are geared towards revenue collection and not road safety.

Layton: And I'll give you an example. If you're driving with a child in a car, and that child is not in a proper child restraint system, and you get pulled over, you are going to get a fine, which in this case is 1500 and you're going to get demerit points against your name. But if you don't update your details with the authorities, you get a 3000 Rand fine. So when we look at the schedule of all the fines and the offences and the demerit points attached to that, a serious offence, like not wearing a seatbelt, that should carry a very heavy Rand fine and it should carry a lot of demerit points. And that's not the case at the moment.

Fikile Mbalula: Yes people are opposed because they say it is a fundraising scheme of government at the expense of the citizens, but it is not. We have decided that it must eat in your pocket, also, to achieve the result that we focus people, on the important part of being safe on the road.

LINK: But what happens when the traffic offence is not actually yours? Well, you may be in for a surprise. The consequences of an error could have a serious effect on your driving record.

VO: David Claase was astonished when his girlfriend (who we’re calling Sarah as she wishes to remain anonymous) had to pay a R750 fine on the spot at a roadblock.

Dave: A female traffic officer asked my partner for her licence disc card and she said "come please, bring your bankcard, you have an outstanding infringement"
Claire: What? Just straight to the bank card?
Dave: the officer said "I won't give your card back unless you've paid".

Claire: There was no way to get out of that roadblock if she did not pay. ???
Dave: Correct. I said to Sarah, let's jump onto the AARTO website, and see if we can see the infringement". Firstly, the image quality on the website isn't the best, the vehicle in the photo is a four door sedan. And Sarah drives a one series hatchback BMW. The number plate is relatively close. the H and the Ns were swapped around.

Howard: That particular infringement carries five demerit points. She's paid the infringement. And it wasn't even her car.Claire: So automatically when she paid the 750, she would have gotten five demerit points.
Howard: Correct.

VO: Sarah has an impeccable driving record, but under the pending regulations she could easily accrue demerit points unknowingly.

VO: Take Kathy, she drives the same route every day, but the speed limit along a stretch of road has been reduced from 80 kms per hour to 60. She doesn't notice, and exceeds the speed limit by 20 kms per hour for 40 days. According to the amendments it can take up to 60 days to receive an infringement notice - the first time she's made aware of her error. And by then she's notched up fines totalling R56000 and 80 demerits - enough to have her licence suspended for 16 and a quarter years.

Howard: That light at the end of the tunnel is a freight train coming towards you. Learn what the AARTO act is all about. Because you will get caught out if you adopt your old habits.

VO: Every step of the way there are fees for processing documents, orders and actions, starting with the Infringement Penalty Levy of R100.

Layton: So just through the infringement penalty levy, for every 10 million infringements that are issued, the system stands to gather 1 billion Rand.

VO: The onus will fall on road users to continually check their driving status. We invited Rushaan Daniels to examine his driving record with Howard. The last time Rushaan checked was 18 months ago.

Howard: Well, you have incurred nine traffic fines.
Rushaan: Wow!
Claire: Are you in disbelief Rushaan?
Rushaan: Yeah, I can't believe I have more than two. Howard is scaring me a bit there.
Claire: Show him the evidence there Howard.
Howard: Feast your eyes on that sunshine. Under the current system, you would have incurred eight demerit points. And under the new system, you would have incurred 24 demerit points.
Rushaan: Wow.
Howard: Under the current system, you would have donated R5920 to the law enforcement authorities. Under the new system, R18,400.
Rushaan: Wow, I can buy a city golf with 18 000.
Claire: Would Rushaan have his driver's licence right now?
Howard: No, So to reduce this below 15 points, would take four or five years.

LINK: One of the aims of AARTO is to alleviate pressure from the court system. Once a representation has been made and it's been rejected, you will have an opportunity to apply for appeal or review before the tribunal.

Howard: And here's this wonderful tribunal, comprising of nine part time members to preside over around 13 million drivers in South Africa and a further 13 million vehicles. And they're going to replace 714 magistrates courts.

Layton: The bottleneck is going to come in at the Appeals Tribunal, where you've got millions of these people who are appealing those infringement notices, and awaiting an outcome to that.

Fikile Mbalula: We will look at the defects in terms of the AARTO system which, and some of the things we believe that will not work, like what you're pointing at, there's no need to maintain in the system.

VO: And with so much still to get right in AARTO and a looming deadline for July, the Minister dropped a bombshell - he plans to change the system even further, by shaking things up within the Road Traffic Infringement Agency and the Road Traffic Management Corporation.

Fikile Mbalula: I'm looking at even rationalisation which will bring RTIA under RTMC, because to me it's a duplication.

VO: With all these billions pouring into the fiscus, how much will actually go to improving hazardous road conditions and overall road safety?

Layton: We've got currently 14,000 people who die on our roads every year and unless we address that holistically, we will never achieve our goals of halving the road deaths by 2030. We need a proper demerit system, which is implemented correctly, and is backed by proper and efficient law enforcement.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 14 April 2021 Press Release: The AARTO Amendment Act for administering road traffic offences in South Africa is due for national rollout in July. The new system includes a points demerit system but is it designed to rid our roads of bad drivers or to fill government coffers? Script: LINK: South African drivers are familiar with receiving traffic fines,// but some of these fines are never enforced, remain unpaid, or are disputed in a court of law.// VO: And motorists like this think they can get away with breaking the law. LINK: On the 1st of July 2021, the AARTO Amendment Act will come into force nationally, changing everything we know about traffic violation enforcement.FX break Are you ready for the impact? Fikile Mbalula: - We are going now to implement a demerit system, if you are going to commit a number of offences… you risk losing your drivers licence. VO: Minister of Transport, Fikile Mbalula, warns South African motorists that they will have to face the strong arm of the law. Fikile Mbalula: Because in SA motorists have a blank cheque they can do as they wish, it doesn't cost them their licence it doesn't cost them anything. VO: Howard Dembovsky, Chairperson for the Justice Project South Africa, is a tireless campaigner for ethical and equitable road traffic law and enforcement. He is opposed to the way AARTO, the Administrative Adjudication of Road Traffic Offences, is being implemented. Howard: What do people ordinarily do when they get a traffic fine in the post? They scrunch it up and throw it in file 13. Claire: Correct Howard: But This administrative system, if you do not act, your failure to act then prejudices you. VO: The JPSA is inundated with requests from motorists unable to sort out their traffic violations like Yulan Chetty,a Joburg resident. He was flummoxed when he couldn't renew his vehicle licence at the post office. Yulan: I was told to go to the traffic department where I was presented with an A4 sheet of about 24 enforcement orders in my name. Claire: 24? Yulan: They were all for the same offence. It was parking outside Gautrain station. it amounted to about R12,000. VO: Yulan is one of around 4 million drivers who have been guinea pigs under the AARTO pilot study in Joburg and Tshwane since 2008, where traffic violations are categorised into infringements, vetted through an administrative process, and offences - tried through the judicial system. Howard: So if you caught driving under the influence of alcohol, you're going to be prosecuted in a criminal court. VO: A parking fine is considered an infringement. Howard: The most significant part of the AARTO Act is migrating Road Traffic offences out of the realm of criminal courts and into an administrative process, which is unfortunately turned into a huge money making exercise. Claire: Was there no piece of paper that they left that they said you've got a ticket? Yulan: There was nothing, nothing. Claire: What if I do not get that fine in the mail? Howard: The AARTO act says it's presumed to be served on the tenth day after it's posted. You may make a written representation that the infringement notice was not served on you. VO: In Yulan’s case, he'd never received infringement notices from the responsible issuing authorities, nor the mandatory courtesy letters from the RTIA, the Road Traffic Infringement Agency. Howard advised Yulan that the only way to appeal was via the AARTO website. And after having to submit 24 certified written representations, eventually all of his fines were revoked. Yulan: It took me eight months to get my licence. I still had to pay the penalties. Even though the enforcement orders were withdrawn. Layton: The purpose of AARTO essentially is to improve road safety and to improve compliance amongst drivers. So the principle behind the introduction of AARTO is something that we support. VO: Layton Beard is the spokesperson for the AA South Africa. Layton: And the introduction of a demerit system is something that the AA supports, but in its current format, that's where we got the problems that come in. VO: The legislation provides that If you accrue over 15 demerits your licence gets suspended for three months for each point over 15. Demerits are reduced at 1 point every 3 months. Third strike and you're out. Your licence is cancelled. // VO: The AA favours a stricter threshold of 12 demerits. They say the proposed amendments are geared towards revenue collection and not road safety. Layton: And I'll give you an example. If you're driving with a child in a car, and that child is not in a proper child restraint system, and you get pulled over, you are going to get a fine, which in this case is 1500 and you're going to get demerit points against your name. But if you don't update your details with the authorities, you get a 3000 Rand fine. So when we look at the schedule of all the fines and the offences and the demerit points attached to that, a serious offence, like not wearing a seatbelt, that should carry a very heavy Rand fine and it should carry a lot of demerit points. And that's not the case at the moment. Fikile Mbalula: Yes people are opposed because they say it is a fundraising scheme of government at the expense of the citizens, but it is not. We have decided that it must eat in your pocket, also, to achieve the result that we focus people, on the important part of being safe on the road. LINK: But what happens when the traffic offence is not actually yours? Well, you may be in for a surprise. The consequences of an error could have a serious effect on your driving record. VO: David Claase was astonished when his girlfriend (who we’re calling Sarah as she wishes to remain anonymous) had to pay a R750 fine on the spot at a roadblock. Dave: A female traffic officer asked my partner for her licence disc card and she said "come please, bring your bankcard, you have an outstanding infringement" Claire: What? Just straight to the bank card? Dave: the officer said "I won't give your card back unless you've paid". Claire: There was no way to get out of that roadblock if she did not pay. ??? Dave: Correct. I said to Sarah, let's jump onto the AARTO website, and see if we can see the infringement". Firstly, the image quality on the website isn't the best, the vehicle in the photo is a four door sedan. And Sarah drives a one series hatchback BMW. The number plate is relatively close. the H and the Ns were swapped around. Howard: That particular infringement carries five demerit points. She's paid the infringement. And it wasn't even her car.Claire: So automatically when she paid the 750, she would have gotten five demerit points. Howard: Correct. VO: Sarah has an impeccable driving record, but under the pending regulations she could easily accrue demerit points unknowingly. VO: Take Kathy, she drives the same route every day, but the speed limit along a stretch of road has been reduced from 80 kms per hour to 60. She doesn't notice, and exceeds the speed limit by 20 kms per hour for 40 days. According to the amendments it can take up to 60 days to receive an infringement notice - the first time she's made aware of her error. And by then she's notched up fines totalling R56000 and 80 demerits - enough to have her licence suspended for 16 and a quarter years. Howard: That light at the end of the tunnel is a freight train coming towards you. Learn what the AARTO act is all about. Because you will get caught out if you adopt your old habits. VO: Every step of the way there are fees for processing documents, orders and actions, starting with the Infringement Penalty Levy of R100. Layton: So just through the infringement penalty levy, for every 10 million infringements that are issued, the system stands to gather 1 billion Rand. VO: The onus will fall on road users to continually check their driving status. We invited Rushaan Daniels to examine his driving record with Howard. The last time Rushaan checked was 18 months ago. Howard: Well, you have incurred nine traffic fines. Rushaan: Wow! Claire: Are you in disbelief Rushaan? Rushaan: Yeah, I can't believe I have more than two. Howard is scaring me a bit there. Claire: Show him the evidence there Howard. Howard: Feast your eyes on that sunshine. Under the current system, you would have incurred eight demerit points. And under the new system, you would have incurred 24 demerit points. Rushaan: Wow. Howard: Under the current system, you would have donated R5920 to the law enforcement authorities. Under the new system, R18,400. Rushaan: Wow, I can buy a city golf with 18 000. Claire: Would Rushaan have his driver's licence right now? Howard: No, So to reduce this below 15 points, would take four or five years. LINK: One of the aims of AARTO is to alleviate pressure from the court system. Once a representation has been made and it's been rejected, you will have an opportunity to apply for appeal or review before the tribunal. Howard: And here's this wonderful tribunal, comprising of nine part time members to preside over around 13 million drivers in South Africa and a further 13 million vehicles. And they're going to replace 714 magistrates courts. Layton: The bottleneck is going to come in at the Appeals Tribunal, where you've got millions of these people who are appealing those infringement notices, and awaiting an outcome to that. Fikile Mbalula: We will look at the defects in terms of the AARTO system which, and some of the things we believe that will not work, like what you're pointing at, there's no need to maintain in the system. VO: And with so much still to get right in AARTO and a looming deadline for July, the Minister dropped a bombshell - he plans to change the system even further, by shaking things up within the Road Traffic Infringement Agency and the Road Traffic Management Corporation. Fikile Mbalula: I'm looking at even rationalisation which will bring RTIA under RTMC, because to me it's a duplication. VO: With all these billions pouring into the fiscus, how much will actually go to improving hazardous road conditions and overall road safety? Layton: We've got currently 14,000 people who die on our roads every year and unless we address that holistically, we will never achieve our goals of halving the road deaths by 2030. We need a proper demerit system, which is implemented correctly, and is backed by proper and efficient law enforcement.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Amendment to the AARTO Act, currently only covering Johannesburg and Tshwane, will become countrywide on July 1st and stakeholders are warning of total gridlock and damaging life consequences.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Because it's a pilot phase the points demerit system of the AARTO system doesn't apply yet, the Minister of Transport has not proclaimed the points demerit system to be in force. But this year the Government is instigating a revolution in AARTO, heralded as a mechanism for improving road safety and a way to ease the burden on courts. The Administrative Adjudication of Road Traffic Offences is to be centralized and will adjudicate countrywide. But what it really could mean is, whatever you thought you knew about traffic offences, think again. The Amendment to the AARTO Act, which currently only has jurisdiction in Johannesburg and Tshwane, is timetabled to be rolled out on July 1st 2021 and automobile stakeholders are warning of total bureaucratic gridlock and damaging life consequences brought on by a skewed system driven by revenue collection, as opposed to road safety.
metadata.Summary: Currently in Johannesburg and Tswane they have been recording demerit points but not enforcing any consequences regarding the points although fines for traffic infringements still have to be paid. So for our story - the consequences regarding the demerit points system have to be hypothetical at this stage, but we do have real life case studies that will show how their current infringements, be they actual or erroneous as in the incorrect number plate case study, could mean under the demerits point sytem and it's administrative pitfalls they would have their licences suspended. Re-enactment August 2021. Mr Joe Soap travels this road every day to and from work. He doesn't realize, because of inadequate notices, that last week the JMPD changed the speed limit of a short stretch of her route from 80 to 60 kilometres per hour. In 40 working days he will have racked up R 56 000 in fines (not to mention the R 100 payment, the Infringement Penalty Levy (IPL),for the privilege of receiving each fine) and 80 demerit points, enough to be banned from driving for 16 and a quarter years. All because there is a speed camera there and it can take up to 60 days for the notification of offences (if they arrive). The AARTO amendments is a strict consequence-based points system. The AARTO Act has effectively three documents 1. Infringement notice, recording the offence 2. Courtesy letter, a reminder to pay 3. Enforcement order, recording the offences consequences and non-payment penalties There are no Warrants of Arrest, no Administration Marks.
metadata.Further information: Skewed penalties and Life Consequences As Howard Dembovsky (of Justice Project South Africa) says, before you even become aware of the fact that that you've been committing traffic offences your license is gone. On the other hand, the drunk driver who drives slowly, because he's trying to follow the dotted lines on the road, he doesn't build up these speeding demerit points, rather he needs to get arrested and convicted nine times before he loses his license. And what of Joe Soap's right to appeal? Well, The AARTO Amendment's appeal process is governed by a tribunal panel of 9 people, at least six of which sit for each appeal. These nine cover the whole country, 13 million driving license holders and a further 13 million registered vehicles. A recipe for Gridlock if people realize that if they appeal every notice of infringement there is no way the Tribunal Panel can keep up. So the claim that AARTO will take the strain off of the courts, really means it just transfers the pressure to another body, it's own Tribunal system. Nine people to do the work of 749 lower courts! And there's more, like, you buy a vehicle from a person and pay them good money for it. And then you can't register the vehicle in your name. Why? Because it can't be taken out of the seller's name because licensing transactions are blocked by an AARTO enforcement order. Also, it is the Insurance Companies' plan to access your demerit points as the insured person and adjust your premium according to the number of demerit points that you have. But when when your insurance premiums become unaffordable, are you going to continue being insured, so the 35% of drivers currently insured may well drop in number. Extra information We will highlight other scenarios that highlight the discrepancy between preaching road safety but practicing maximizing revenue. Like, the R 3000 fine for not updating authorities on where you live, compared with a R 500 fine and 1 demerit point for transporting your baby by car without sitting them safely in a car baby chair. Howard Dembovsky has a database of all the offences and consequences for us to access further comparisons of the weighting of certain offenses. Are there alternative solutions? Howard Dembovsky suggests: scrap the AARTO Act and incorporate the points demerit system into the National Road Traffic Act and establish a dedicated 24 hours per day traffic court. Howard Dembovsky is also willing to surprise the presenter by revealing to them their current traffic offenses record and the consequences of those under the AARTO Act Amendment. Possible case study: Older Lady - Gladys Rankhumise - Mini bus taxis were registered in her name without her knowledge: Enforcement orders issued against her in respect of those mini bus taxis prevented her from renewing her driver's licence. Under the demerit system she would also not have been aware that these demerits were notching up against her name, because they were being sent to a false address. In this instance she filled in the prescribed form, submited it to the agency for consideration, they rejected her submission, and had she not been able to get someone to help her argue her case, like Howard, she would have to get herself a lawyer, because under the new system once an enforecement order has been issued you can no longer apply to the tribunal for appeal. She would have to institute a PAJA application to the high court, which would cost her no less than a million Rand. Under the new system.. once the enforcement order has been issued she is left with two options either pay the outstanding enforcement orders, which she was not actually liable for which maybe amounted to, say R5000 or R 7000 or pay for the High Court and find a million Rand. Most people would opt for option 1, even if they were not at fault. Currently those demerit points are not in force, but the department is apparently monitoring them. Demerit points are applied when you pay the fine, or when you are found guilty in a court of law or when an enforcement order is issued. Demerit points decrease at the rate of 1 point every three months .
